mainTopic: Following the stringencies of two opinions, and how to fix an alley that is open at both ends
overview: The גמרא finishes explaining a ברייתא that says the הלכה follows בית הלל, yet lets a person act like בית שמאי. It then rules out taking the leniencies of both sides, or the stringencies of both sides. The alleyway in נהרדעא, which was treated with the stringencies of both רב and שמואל, still seems to break that rule. רב נחמן בר יצחק answers that everything there followed רב, who held 'הלכה ואין מורין כן'. When another version of רב's words undoes that answer, רב שיזבי limits the rule: we avoid two stringencies only when they contradict each other, like the spine in טומאה and in טריפה. A challenge from רבי עקיבא's two tithes is answered: he was strict both ways because he was in doubt. Then the גמרא returns to the מבוי מפולש. רב defines when the dispute applies (main street or plaza on both sides) and when a lighter fix is enough (a valley on one or both sides). A final ruling says an alley ending in an enclosed yard needs nothing at that end, and אביי identifies that ruling as שמואל's.

steps.title: The clause allowing one to follow בית שמאי reflects רבי יהושע, who ignores a בת קול
steps.stepSummary: The previous answer ends by saying that the clause of the ברייתא that lets a person follow בית שמאי reflects the view of רבי יהושע, who does not accept a בת קול as deciding הלכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And that part of the ברייתא follows רבי יהושע, who does not pay attention to a בת קול.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer it began on the previous amud. It explains that one part of the ברייתא follows רבי יהושע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בת קול announced that the הלכה follows בית הלל, so a clause letting one act like בית שמאי seems impossible after it. If you ignore the בת קול, as רבי יהושע does, the dispute between בית שמאי and בית הלל is still open. That is why this clause can still let a person choose בית שמאי's view.

keyTerms.meaning: A Heavenly Voice
Does not pay attention to
The תנא who held that a בת קול does not decide הלכה

steps.confusionAlert: This line is the end of an answer that started on the previous amud. It is not a brand-new statement.

phrases.english: And it is the view of Rabbi Yehoshua
phrases.notes: Refers to the latter clause of the ברייתא.

phrases.english: who does not pay attention to a Heavenly Voice.
phrases.notes: So for him the dispute was never decided by the בת קול.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ הִיא דְּלָא מַשְׁגַּח בְּבַת קוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes an answer that began on the previous amud.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attribution of a clause to a specific תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא contradicts itself, since one part says the הלכה always follows בית הלל and another part allows a person to act like בית שמאי.
steps.terutzMaskana: The clause that allows acting like בית שמאי follows רבי יהושע, who ignores the בת קול.

steps.title: Another reading: do not mix and match leniencies or stringencies
steps.stepSummary: A different reading of the ברייתא: what it forbids is mixing the leniencies of both opinions, or the stringencies of both opinions. You must follow one opinion consistently, taking both its leniencies and its stringencies.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you could say the ברייתא means this. Whenever two תנאים or two אמוראים argue the way בית שמאי and בית הלל do, do not take the leniency of one and the leniency of the other. Also do not take the stringency of one and the stringency of the other. Instead, follow one opinion in both its leniencies and its stringencies, or follow the other opinion in both.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second way to understand the ברייתא. Its point is about consistency, not about which side wins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In disputes structured like those of בית שמאי and בית הלל, one side is lenient on one issue and the other side is lenient on another. Picking all the leniencies, or all the stringencies, combines positions that contradict each other. The rule is to pick one opinion and follow it all the way.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces another answer)
His leniency
His stringency
Of the Master (one of the disputing opinions)
Sages of the משנה period and Sages of the גמרא period

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a lasting principle in פסק: you may not combine contradictory positions of two opinions, whether to be lenient or to be strict.
steps.confusionAlert: The problem is not being strict. The problem is mixing two opinions that contradict each other. Following one opinion's stringencies together with its leniencies is fine.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say: this is what it is saying:
Wherever you find
two tanna'im or two amora'im
who disagree with each other

phrases.aramaic: כְּעֵין מַחֲלוֹקֶת בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וּבֵית הִלֵּל —
phrases.english: in the manner of the disputes of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
one should not act like the leniency of one Master
and like the leniency of the other Master,
nor like the stringency of one Master
and like the stringency of the other Master.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא, אוֹ כִּי קוּלֵּיהּ דְּמָר וּכְחוּמְרֵיהּ עָבֵיד,
phrases.english: Rather, either he acts like one Master's leniency and his stringency,
or he acts like the other Master's leniency and his stringency.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer, replacing the answer that attributed the clause to רבי יהושע.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא speaks about בית שמאי and בית הלל themselves, so letting one follow בית שמאי clashes with the בת קול.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about any two disputants who argue like בית שמאי and בית הלל. One may follow either one consistently, but may not mix their leniencies or their stringencies.

steps.title: Either way, the נהרדעא alleyway is still a problem
steps.stepSummary: Whichever reading of the ברייתא we use, the alleyway in נהרדעא was treated with the stringencies of both רב and שמואל, and that is still difficult.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to its original problem. Both readings of the ברייתא still forbid what was done with the alleyway in נהרדעא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two answers only explained the wording of the ברייתא. They did not justify the practice in נהרדעא, which combined the stringencies of רב and of שמואל. That practice remains a contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: In any case / either way
It is difficult

phrases.english: In any case, it is difficult!
phrases.notes: Refers to the alleyway in נהרדעא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the readings of the ברייתא but says the original question still stands.
steps.kashyaTarget: The practice in the alleyway of נהרדעא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under either reading, combining the stringencies of both רב and שמואל is forbidden, yet that is what was done in נהרדעא.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק: they followed רב entirely
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers that the alleyway in נהרדעא was handled completely according to רב, not as a mix of רב and שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: they did the whole thing according to רב.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers the difficulty. He denies that two opinions were combined at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If everything done in נהרדעא fits רב's view alone, then nobody mixed opinions, and the ברייתא is not violated. The requirement of דלתות, which looked like an extra stringency, still needs to be explained according to רב. The next step does that.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who gives the answer
All of it / entirely
They did it / acted

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
They did all of it according to Rav.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: כּוּלֵּיהּ כְּרַב עַבְדוּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the difficulty raised in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reattribution: all of the practice follows one opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: נהרדעא combined the stringencies of רב and of שמואל.
steps.terutzMaskana: Everything in נהרדעא follows רב alone, so no opinions were mixed.

steps.title: רב's rule: it is the הלכה, but we do not teach it publicly
steps.stepSummary: The support for the answer: רב said that the lenient rule is the הלכה, but it is not taught to the public. So requiring דלתות is itself part of רב's position.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב הונא said in the name of רב: it is the הלכה, but we do not rule that way publicly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source that shows the stringency in נהרדעא came from רב himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב holds that a צורת הפתח is enough for an open מבוי. However, he says this is not taught publicly, so in practice people are told to make דלתות. Requiring doors therefore fits רב's own view and is not borrowed from someone else.

keyTerms.meaning: Student of רב who transmits his teaching
It is the הלכה, but we do not rule that way publicly
Teach / issue a ruling

steps.whatToRemember: The נהרדעא practice did not mix opinions. Following רב, the lenient law (צורת הפתח is enough) is true, but publicly the ruling is strict (require דלתות). So everything came from רב.
steps.confusionAlert: "הלכה ואין מורין כן" does not mean רב was unsure. The lenient law is correct, but it is not announced publicly as a ruling.
steps.whyThisMatters: This introduces the important category of הלכה ואין מורין כן: a law can be true and still not be taught publicly as a practical ruling.

phrases.english: As Rav Huna said that Rav said:
It is the halacha, but we do not instruct so.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב: הֲלָכָה וְאֵין מוֹרִין כֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source that backs רב נחמן בר יצחק's claim.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that the stringency in נהרדעא follows רב alone
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב הונא's report in the name of רב: הלכה ואין מורין כן

steps.title: The other version of רב's ruling brings the problem back
steps.stepSummary: According to רב אדא בר אהבה, רב said the lenient view is the הלכה and is taught publicly. So requiring doors cannot be explained as part of רב's own view.
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to רב אדא בר אהבה, who quoted רב as saying 'this is the הלכה and we teach it publicly,' what can we say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from steps 4-5 by bringing a different report of what רב said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 worked because in that report רב held the lenient rule but would not teach it publicly, so being strict in practice was still 'pure רב.' In רב אדא בר אהבה's report, רב openly teaches the leniency. In that case, being strict in נהרדעא is no longer רב's position, and we are back to mixing the stringencies of רב and שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who reports a different version of רב's ruling
It is the הלכה, and we teach it to the public
What can be said? (a formula that introduces a challenge)

phrases.aramaic: וּלְרַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה אָמַר רַב,
phrases.english: And according to Rav Adda bar Ahava, who reported in the name of Rav,
who said: it is the halacha, and we rule that way publicly,
what is there to say?
phrases.notes: In other words, why did נהרדעא take on both sets of stringencies?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the support in step 5 by quoting a different version of רב's statement.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן בר יצחק's answer that the alley in נהרדעא followed רב alone
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If רב teaches the leniency publicly, then being strict is not part of his view. The practice in נהרדעא becomes a mix of רב and שמואל again.

steps.title: The rule only applies when the two stringencies contradict
steps.stepSummary: רב שיזבי limits the rule. We avoid adopting both opinions' stringencies only when those stringencies contradict each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שיזבי said: The case where we do not follow the stringencies of two opinions is only where they contradict each other.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שיזבי answers the challenge by narrowing the rule against taking both stringencies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking both stringencies is not a problem in itself. The problem arises only when being strict like both opinions forces you into a logical contradiction. The two stringencies in נהרדעא do not clash with each other, so adopting both is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who gives this answer
The stringencies of two (opposing) authorities
They contradict one another

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the boundary of the principle against mixing opinions. Being strict like both sides is a problem only when it is logically inconsistent.

phrases.english: Rav Sheizvi said:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי לָא עָבְדִינַן כְּחוּמְרֵי דְּבֵי תְרֵי —
phrases.english: when we do not act according to the stringencies of two authorities
that is where they contradict one another.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁיזְבִי: כִּי לָא עָבְדִינַן כְּחוּמְרֵי דְּבֵי תְרֵי
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of a rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any adoption of both opinions' stringencies is forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: Adopting both stringencies is forbidden only when they contradict each other. נהרדעא's practice did not involve a contradiction.

steps.title: Example: the spine and skull of a dead body
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה as an example. בית שמאי and בית הלל argue about how much must be missing from a spine or skull before it stops causing טומאת אהל.
steps.simpleTranslation: For example, the spine and the skull. As we learned in a משנה: a spine or skull that is missing a part. How much must be missing? For the spine, בית שמאי say two vertebrae, and בית הלל say one vertebra. For the skull, בית שמאי say a hole the size of a drill, and בית הלל say enough that if it were taken from a living person, he would die.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins to illustrate what a 'contradicting' stringency looks like. This step sets up the example, and the next step completes it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A complete spine or skull causes טומאה through a tent, but a defective one does not. For the spine, בית שמאי require two missing vertebrae, so they are stricter for טומאה, while בית הלל treat one missing vertebra as defective. For the skull it flips: בית שמאי count even a drill-sized hole as defective, while בית הלל require a large, fatal-sized gap, so בית הלל are stricter for טומאה.

keyTerms.meaning: Spine
Skull
Vertebra / vertebrae
The size of a drill hole
As we learned in a משנה

steps.confusionAlert: Here, 'missing more' means the bone becomes LESS טמא, because it is no longer a complete spine or skull. So the view that requires a bigger loss is the stricter view for טומאה.

phrases.english: For example, a spine and a skull.
As we learned: a spine or skull that is missing a part
phrases.notes: Such a bone does not cause טומאה through a tent.

phrases.english: And how much counts as missing?

phrases.aramaic: בַּשִּׁדְרָה, בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: שְׁתֵּי חוּלְיוֹת,
phrases.english: For the spine, Beit Shammai say: two vertebrae,
and Beit Hillel say: one vertebra.

phrases.aramaic: וּבַגּוּלְגּוֹלֶת, בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: כִּמְלֹא מַקְדֵּחַ,
phrases.english: And for the skull, Beit Shammai say: the size of a drill hole,

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּנָּטֵל מִן הַחַי וְיָמוּת.
phrases.english: and Beit Hillel say: enough that, if removed from a living person, he would die.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the kind of contradiction רב שיזבי means in step 7.
steps.raayaObject: רב שיזבי's idea of stringencies that contradict each other
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about a defective spine and skull (in אהלות)

steps.title: The same argument applies to טריפה, which creates the contradiction
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says בית שמאי and בית הלל have the same argument about טריפה. Being strict in both טומאה and טריפה would define the same bone loss in two opposite ways.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: the same argument applies to טריפה.
steps.whatsHappening: This completes the example. The same measurements decide whether an animal is a טריפה, so now we can see the contradiction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For טריפה, counting a spine as 'defective' is the strict side, because it makes the animal forbidden. If someone is strict like בית הלל for טריפה (one missing vertebra makes the spine defective) and strict like בית שמאי for טומאה (one missing vertebra does not make the spine defective), he is treating the same spine as both defective and not defective. That is a true contradiction, and that is what the rule forbids. The case in נהרדעא had no such clash.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect, forbidden to eat even after שחיטה
And the same applies to the subject of
רב יהודה reporting in the name of שמואל

steps.whatToRemember: We may follow the stringencies of two opinions together, unless doing so makes us treat the same reality in two opposite ways, like the spine in טומאה and in טריפה.

phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel:
and the same applies to the laws of a tereifa.
phrases.notes: Here 'defective' is the strict side, the opposite of טומאה.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: וְכֵן לְעִנְיַן טְרֵיפָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the example begun in step 8 by showing where the contradiction comes from.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית שמאי and בית הלל's measures for a defective spine and skull also decide whether an animal is a טריפה. So being strict in both areas would be self-contradictory.

steps.title: Two stringencies that do not clash are allowed
steps.stepSummary: רב שיזבי completes his limitation: when two stringencies do not contradict each other, we may follow both.
steps.simpleTranslation: But where the two stringencies do not contradict each other, we do follow both.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רב שיזבי's answer from Step 7. Two stringencies that do not clash may both be followed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 said we avoid both stringencies only when they contradict each other. This line states the other side: if they don't clash, adopting both is fine. That explains the alley in נהרדעא, where רב's stringency and שמואל's stringency dealt with two separate issues.

keyTerms.meaning: They contradict each other
We do act (this way)

steps.whatToRemember: The rule: you may follow two stringencies if they don't contradict each other. You may not follow them if they do.

phrases.english: But where they do not contradict each other
we do act (according to both).

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל הֵיכָא דְּלָא סָתְרִי אַהֲדָדֵי עָבְדִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב שיזבי's limitation, after the טומאה/טריפה example of a contradiction in Steps 8-9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of a rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think following two opinions' stringencies is never allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is forbidden only when the stringencies contradict each other. Otherwise it is allowed.

steps.title: Challenge from רבי עקיבא's two tithes
steps.stepSummary: רב משרשיא challenges the rule. רבי עקיבא followed both בית שמאי and בית הלל on an אתרוג, even though their views contradict.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it true that where the stringencies contradict each other we do not follow both? רב משרשיא objected: There was a story with רבי עקיבא. He picked an אתרוג on the first of שבט and separated two tithes from it. He separated one according to בית שמאי and one according to בית הלל!
steps.whatsHappening: רב משרשיא attacks רב שיזבי's rule. He brings a story where רבי עקיבא seems to follow two contradicting opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For בית שמאי, ראש השנה לאילנות is א' בשבט, so the אתרוג belongs to the new year. For בית הלל it is ט"ו בשבט, so the fruit still belongs to the old year. Each year requires a different tithe, מעשר שני or מעשר עני. Separating both treats the fruit as new-year and old-year at once, which is a direct contradiction. Yet רבי עקיבא did it.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises an objection (from a source)
Citron fruit
The month whose date marks the new year for trees
Tithes (here מַעֲשֵׂר שֵׁנִי and מַעֲשֵׂר עָנִי)

steps.confusionAlert: Only one of the two tithes is really required. Which one depends on which year the fruit belongs to. Doing both treats the fruit as belonging to both years.

phrases.english: And where they contradict each other we do not act?!
Rav Mesharshiya raised an objection:
There was an incident with Rabbi Akiva
who picked a citron on the first of Shevat,
and applied two tithes to it:
one according to the words of Beit Shammai,
and one according to the words of Beit Hillel?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהֵיכָא דְּסָתְרִי אַהֲדָדֵי לָא עָבְדִינַן מֵתִיב רַב מְשַׁרְשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the rule just stated in Steps 7 and 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב שיזבי's rule that we don't follow two contradicting stringencies
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי עקיבא followed both בית שמאי and בית הלל on the date of the trees' new year. Their positions contradict, so contradicting stringencies were followed in practice.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא was in doubt, not combining opinions
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא was unsure whether בית הלל said א' בשבט or ט"ו בשבט, so he was strict both ways out of doubt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא was unsure about what he had learned. He did not know whether בית הלל said the first of שבט or the fifteenth of שבט. So he acted strictly here and strictly there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. רבי עקיבא was not choosing to follow two opinions. He was unsure of the facts of בית הלל's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If בית הלל also said א' בשבט, there is no argument, and the fruit is new-year fruit. If בית הלל said ט"ו בשבט, the fruit is old-year fruit. Since he did not know which was true, being strict both ways is a normal way to handle a doubt (ספק). It is not the forbidden practice of collecting stringencies from opposing opinions.

keyTerms.meaning: His learned tradition
He was in doubt
Stringently
A doubt

steps.whatToRemember: Being strict both ways because of a real doubt is different from mixing the stringencies of two opposing views.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up an important distinction: being strict out of uncertainty is legitimate, even when the two stringencies look contradictory.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva was in doubt about his tradition,
and did not know whether Beit Hillel
said the first of Shevat,
or said the fifteenth of Shevat,
so he acted stringently here and stringently there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב משרשיא's challenge and defends רב שיזבי's rule.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (a doubt rather than following two opinions)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי עקיבא knowingly adopted the stringencies of both בית שמאי and בית הלל.
steps.terutzMaskana: He was unsure what בית הלל held, so being strict both ways was a way of handling the doubt.

steps.title: רב defines the case of the open-alley dispute
steps.stepSummary: Back to alleys open at both ends: רב says the dispute is about an alley with a main street on both sides, or a plaza on both sides.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף sat before רב הונא, and he sat and said: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: The dispute is where there is a main street on this side and a main street on that side. It is also where there is a plaza on this side and a plaza on that side.
steps.whatsHappening: The side discussion about stringencies is over. The גמרא now returns to the earlier topic, the alley open at both ends (מבוי מפולש). This step defines exactly which case the earlier dispute is about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier there was a dispute between the תנא קמא and חנניה over how to fix an alley that is open at both ends. רב now says that dispute applies when both ends open onto the same kind of public area. That means a main street (סרטיא) on both sides, or a plaza (פלטיא) on both sides.

keyTerms.meaning: Sat before him (as a student)
The dispute
A main street (public thoroughfare)
A plaza / open public square
From here, on this side

phrases.aramaic: יָתֵיב רַב יוֹסֵף קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב הוּנָא,
phrases.english: Rav Yosef sat before Rav Huna,
and he sat and said,
Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
The dispute is where there is a main street on this side and a main street on that side,
or a plaza on this side and a plaza on that side.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָתֵיב רַב יוֹסֵף קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב הוּנָא וְיָתֵיב וְקָאָמַר אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side discussion about stringencies and returns to the main topic of the מבוי מפולש.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The dispute over the open alley applies when both ends open onto a main street, or both ends open onto a plaza.

steps.title: When a valley is on one or both sides, a lighter fix is enough
steps.stepSummary: רב continues: if one side of the alley opens to a main street and the other to a valley, or both sides open to valleys, a doorway-frame on one end and a side post or beam on the other end is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if there is a main street on one side and a valley on the other side, or a valley on both sides, you make a doorway-frame on one side and a side post or beam on the other side.
steps.whatsHappening: רב is finishing the statement from the last step. He now describes the easier cases, where at least one side of the alley opens to a valley instead of a main street.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the last step, the dispute was about an alley with a main street on both sides, which is the hard case. Here רב says that once a valley (בקעה) is involved, you do not need a doorway-frame on both ends. A doorway-frame on one end and a simple side post or beam on the other end is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: A main public street, a true public domain
An open valley or field, treated as a כַּרְמְלִית (an in-between area where carrying is forbidden by the Rabbis)
A doorway-frame: two posts with a beam across the top
A single side post placed at the alley's opening
A beam placed across the top of the alley's opening

phrases.english: But a main street on this side
and a valley on that side,
or a valley on this side and a valley on that side —
one makes a doorway-frame on this side
and a side post or a beam on that side.
phrases.notes: The ו here means 'or': either a side post or a beam is enough.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב's statement from step 13 by setting the easier cases against the main-street-on-both-sides case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Main street plus valley, or valley plus valley: a doorway-frame on one end and a side post or beam on the other end is enough.

steps.title: Why say the obvious case of valleys on both sides?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if a main street plus a valley needs only the lighter fix, then valleys on both sides is surely enough too. Why did רב need to say it?
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, if a main street on one side and a valley on the other only needs a doorway-frame on one side and a side post or beam on the other, does it even need to be said about a valley on both sides?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges how רב's words are built. The second case seems obvious once the first case is known.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A main street is the stricter situation and a valley is the milder one. If the stricter mix (main street plus valley) already gets the lighter fix, then the milder case (valley plus valley) obviously does too. So listing it seems extra.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Now', the opening of an 'if this, then surely that' argument
'Is it necessary to say?', meaning the point is obvious
An alley open at both ends

phrases.english: Now, if a main street on this side and a valley on that side
one makes for it a doorway-frame on this side
and a side post or beam on that side —
then a valley on this side and a valley on that side — does that even need to be said?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording of step 14 because it seems to say something unnecessary.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's listing of 'a valley on both sides' as a separate case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the stricter case gets the lighter fix, the milder case obviously does too, so the second case is extra.

steps.title: Main street plus valley counts as valleys on both sides
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רב was not listing two separate cases. He meant that a main street plus a valley is treated exactly like a valley on both sides.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he means: a main street on one side and a valley on the other side is treated like a valley on both sides.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by reading רב's words differently. The case of valleys on both sides is the model case, and the mixed case is being compared to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, it looked like רב was listing two cases, one of them obvious. Now the words 'or a valley on both sides' are read as 'it becomes like a valley on both sides.' The new point is that one valley side is enough to take the alley out of the strict main-street-on-both-sides category.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This is what he means', a re-reading of an earlier statement
'Becomes like', meaning it is treated the same as

phrases.english: This is what he means:
a main street on this side and a valley on that side
is treated like a valley on this side and a valley on that side.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 15 by re-reading רב's wording.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading (הכי קאמר): the second phrase is a comparison, not a separate case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב listed two separate cases, and the second one was obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב taught one case: main street plus valley is treated like valleys on both sides.
steps.whatToRemember: An alley that is open at both ends is only in the strict category when a main street is on both sides. Once one side opens to a valley, it is treated like valleys on both sides: a doorway-frame on one end and a side post or beam on the other end.

steps.title: An alley ending in an enclosed yard needs nothing at that end
steps.stepSummary: A closing ruling in the name of רב יהודה: if the alley ends in an enclosed back-yard (רחבה), that end needs no post, beam, or doorway-frame.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he ended the teaching with this, in the name of רב יהודה: if the alley ended in a back-yard, nothing is needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The one reporting the teaching adds a final ruling in רב יהודה's own name. It covers an alley whose end leads into an enclosed yard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A רחבה here is a closed-off yard behind houses. An alley that ends in it counts as closed on that side, so that end needs no fix at all. This adds a third kind of end to the earlier ones (main street and valley), and it is the most lenient.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And he concluded with it', an added closing statement
'Ends into', the place where the alley comes out
Here, an enclosed back-yard behind a group of houses
'Nothing is needed', no post, beam, or doorway-frame

steps.confusionAlert: Do not confuse this רחבה with an open public plaza. Here it means an enclosed yard behind houses, which is why the alley counts as closed on that side.

phrases.english: And he concluded it in the name of Rav Yehuda:
If the alley ended in a back-yard,
nothing is needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a closing ruling about another kind of alley end, after the main-street and valley cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An alley that ends in an enclosed back-yard needs nothing at that end.
steps.whyThisMatters: It completes the scale of alley ends from strictest to most lenient: main street, then valley, then enclosed yard.

steps.title: אביי identifies the ruling as שמואל's
steps.stepSummary: אביי tells רב יוסף that רב יהודה's ruling about the רחבה comes from שמואל, not from רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רב יוסף: This ruling of רב יהודה is really שמואל's.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי tags the ruling from the last step with its true source. He says רב יהודה learned it from שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה learned from two great teachers, רב and שמואל, so a ruling in his name could come from either one. אביי clarifies that this one is שמואל's. That matters because the ruling may not fit רב's own approach to alleys, which the גמרא just discussed.

keyTerms.meaning: A leading אמורא, student of רב יוסף
אביי's teacher and head of the yeshiva in Pumbedita
"This ruling of...": points back to a statement just quoted
"It is שמואל's": names the true source of a ruling

steps.confusionAlert: אביי is not arguing with the ruling or rejecting it. He is only identifying whose view it is, which helps us see how it fits with רב's statements just before.
steps.whyThisMatters: Knowing that the ruling is שמואל's tells us it may not match רב's approach to alleys, which the גמרא laid out in the steps just before.

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rav Yosef:
This ruling of Rav Yehuda
is Shmuel's.
phrases.notes: It is not the view of רב, רב יהודה's other teacher.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי לְרַב יוֹסֵף: הָא דְּרַב יְהוּדָה דִּשְׁמוּאֵל הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Identifies the source of the רב יהודה ruling quoted in Step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ruling that an alley ending in a רחבה needs no fix at that end follows שמואל, not רב.
